1.open: Think of a time you got a message or a story secondhand and later heard it straight from the source. What was different?
questions: Paul says he was sent "not from men nor by man, but by Jesus Christ and God the Father" (v. 1). Why do you think he opens a letter with this before anything else?
Verse 4 sums up the good news: Jesus "gave Himself for our sins to rescue us from the present evil age." What does the word "rescue" bring to mind for you, and how is it different from "improve"?
Paul is "amazed how quickly" the Galatians are "deserting the One who called you by the grace of Christ" (v. 6). Why do you think people drift from grace so easily, even after they have received it?
Verse 10 asks, "Am I now seeking the approval of men, or of God?" Where do you feel the pull to please people more than to be honest about what you believe?
Paul describes how "severely I persecuted the church of God" and how zealous he was (vv. 13, 14). What does it say about God that he called someone like this "by His grace" (v. 15)?
After God called him, Paul did not rush to consult anyone but went into Arabia (vv. 16, 17). Why might time away and quiet matter when your faith is being shaped? Have you had a season like that?

Christians read the "different gospel" differently. Some see it as earning God's favor by good works, others as requiring non-Jewish believers to become Jewish to belong. Either way, what are some ways people today add something to grace?

The Judean churches heard that the former persecutor was now preaching the faith, "and they glorified God because of me" (vv. 23, 24). If you are unsure or doubting right now, what would it mean to you that God can change a person that much? What feels hard to believe about it?
1.life: Pick one thing you tend to quietly add to the good news, such as thinking you have to earn God's love or that you have to look a certain way to belong. This week, each time it shows up, say out loud or in your head, "Grace and peace to you" (v. 3), and thank God that Christ gave himself for you.
1.prayer: Thank God for the grace that called you, whatever your past looks like. Ask for the freedom to care more about God's approval than people's, and pray for anyone in the group who feels far from God tonight.
1.tip: Verses 8 and 9 sound harsh, and someone may be uncomfortable with the word "curse." Say plainly that Paul is protective of the good news because so much is at stake for the Galatians, not angry at people who struggle. Then steer back to verses 3 to 5 and the grace that frames the whole chapter.

2.open: Think of a time you felt like the outsider at a table, a team or a party. What helped you feel welcome, or what would have?
questions: Paul says some people "had come in under false pretenses to spy on our freedom in Christ Jesus" (v. 4). Why might it matter so much to Paul that Titus not be forced to be circumcised?

The leaders in Jerusalem "added nothing to me" (v. 6) and gave Paul and Barnabas "the right hand of fellowship" (v. 9). What does it look like when people in a church welcome someone without adding extra requirements?
Their only request was to "remember the poor" (v. 10). Why might caring for the poor be a fitting thing to ask of people who are saved by grace?

Peter used to eat with Gentiles, but then "began to draw back and separate himself, for fear of those in the circumcision group" (v. 12). What kinds of fear can make us quietly pull away from people we know we should welcome?
Paul says Peter's actions were not "walking in line with the truth of the gospel" (v. 14). How can where we sit and who we eat with say something about what we believe?

Paul says "a man is not justified by works of the law, but by faith in Jesus Christ" (v. 16). Christians differ on exactly what "works of the law" means here. However you read it, where do you still catch yourself trying to earn God's approval?

Paul writes, "I have been crucified with Christ, and I no longer live, but Christ lives in me" (v. 20). If you are unsure what that means or whether it feels true for you, what questions or hesitations come up?
Paul says Christ "loved me and gave Himself up for me" (v. 20). What changes, even a little, if you hear that as personal and not only general?
2.life: Look for one person at church, work or school who tends to sit on the edge. This week, share a meal or a coffee with them, and notice what it costs you and what it gives.
2.prayer: Thank God that we are made right through trust in Christ and not through our own record. Ask for courage to welcome others as Christ has welcomed us, and for honesty about where we still pull away.
2.tip: Verses 15 to 21 are dense, and people may get stuck on what "justified" or "works of the law" means. Say in one line that Christians read the phrase in different ways, then steer back to the shared point: we are made right by trusting Christ, and everyone is welcome at the table. Verses 11 to 14 also tend to prompt a debate about Paul versus Peter, so remind the group that this is a story about fear and habit, something we all know.

3.open: Think of a group you belonged to, like a team, a club or a family tradition. How did you know you were part of it?
questions: Paul is frustrated and says, "O foolish Galatians!" (v. 1). He asks whether they started "in the Spirit" and are now "finishing in the flesh" (v. 3). Where do people begin with God's grace and then slip into trying to make it on their own effort?

Paul points to Abraham: "Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness" (v. 6). What does it mean to you that trust, not performance, was what God counted? What does trusting God look like on an ordinary Tuesday?
Paul says "Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us" (v. 13). What do you hear in that sentence? Why might it be good news for someone who feels they never measure up?

Christians understand Paul's phrase "works of the law" in different ways. Some hear a rejection of earning God's favor by good deeds, others hear a focus on Jewish markers like circumcision, and some stress that being made right includes real change inside. Where do you find yourself drawn, and what do you want to learn from someone who sees it differently?

Paul says "the law became our guardian to lead us to Christ" (v. 24). He pictures a household minder who walks a child to school and whose job ends when the child grows up. How does that picture change how you think about rules and commands in the Bible?
Paul says we receive God's gifts by trusting. If your own faith feels small, shaky or full of questions right now, what is that like for you? Be as honest as you want. Passing is fine too.

Paul writes, "You are all sons of God through faith in Christ Jesus" (v. 26), and "you are all one in Christ Jesus" (v. 28). Who is hardest for you to picture as an equal member of the family? Christians agree this means equal standing before God but differ on how far it changes roles in church and society. How can your group talk about that kindly?
Verse 27 says believers "have clothed yourselves with Christ." Where does belonging feel like something you had to earn, and where does it feel simply given?
3.life: This week, notice one moment when you are trying to earn approval, from God or from people. Stop and remind yourself quietly that you belong because of Christ, not because of your performance. Then do the next thing from that place.
3.prayer: Thank God that you are his child through faith in Christ. Ask him to loosen your grip on proving yourself, and to help your group welcome everyone as family.
3.tip: Verses 15 to 20 are dense and even scholars find parts of them hard. If the group gets stuck there, say that plainly, name the big point (the promise came first and the law cannot cancel it), and move on to verses 23 to 29, where the chapter lands.

4.open: When you were a kid, what was a rule in your house that you couldn't wait to be old enough to break or outgrow?
questions: Paul says an heir who is still a child is "no different from a slave" until the time his father set (v. 1). What picture is he painting, and what do you think it would have meant to the Galatians?
Verses 4 and 5 say God sent His Son "to redeem those under the law, that we might receive our adoption as sons." What does it mean to you that we are adopted, not just forgiven?

Verse 6 says the Spirit cries out, "Abba, Father!" in our hearts. When you think of God as a father, what comes to mind, and is it easy or hard? Be as honest as you like, including if it feels distant or you're not sure.

Paul asks why they would turn back to "weak and worthless principles" and be "enslaved by them all over again" (v. 9). Why might old rules or expectations feel safer than freedom, even to someone who knows better?
In verses 12 to 15 Paul reminds them how warmly they welcomed him when he was ill. Why do you think he brings up their friendship in the middle of a hard argument?

Verse 17 says some people are "zealous for you, but not in a good way," wanting to isolate the Galatians from Paul. How can you tell the difference between someone who cares for you and someone who is pulling you into their own group?
Paul says he is in labor "until Christ is formed in you" (v. 19). What do you think it looks like for Christ to take shape in an ordinary person over time?
Paul tells them, "you, brothers, like Isaac, are children of promise" (v. 28). What changes in daily life if you see yourself as a child who received a promise, not a worker trying to earn a place?
4.life: Notice one place this week where you act like a servant trying to earn God's approval, such as guilt over a missed habit or a checklist you carry. Each time, remind yourself that you are a son or daughter and not a slave (see v. 7), and talk to God as a Father about it.
4.prayer: Thank God for adopting us and sending His Spirit into our hearts. Ask Him to loosen any rule or fear you are still gripping, and to help Christ take shape in each person in the group.
4.tip: The Hagar and Sarah section (vv. 21 to 31) can feel confusing and even harsh, especially verse 30. Keep it simple: Paul is using the story as a picture of slavery and promise, and many scholars read his strong words as aimed at the rival teachers, not at Jewish people. Also note that Christians differ on whether Paul is rejecting the law as a way to earn standing with God, or rejecting the demand that non-Jews adopt Jewish customs to belong. Name that in a sentence, then return to the heart of the chapter: you are a child, not a slave.

5.open: What is a rule you grew up with that you still follow today, even though nobody is making you?
questions: Paul opens with "It is for freedom that Christ has set us free" (v. 1). What do you think he means by freedom here, and how is that different from doing whatever you like?
Paul warns against being "encumbered once more by a yoke of slavery" (v. 1). What are some modern yokes, spoken or unspoken, that people put on themselves or on each other in the name of faith?
In verse 6 what matters is "faith expressing itself through love." What would that look like on an ordinary Tuesday, at home or at work?

Christians read this chapter differently: some hear a warning against earning God's favor by good deeds, others hear a warning against making Jewish customs a requirement for non-Jewish believers. How might each reading still speak to us today?
Paul says "serve one another in love" and sums up the law as "Love your neighbor as yourself" (vv. 13, 14). Who is one person in your life it is hard to serve this way, and why?
Verse 15 pictures people "biting and devouring one another." How do you see that kind of quarrelling show up in churches, families or online, and what helps stop it?

Verse 17 says the flesh and the Spirit "are opposed to each other, so that you do not do what you want." Where do you feel that tug of war in your own life? Feel free to answer honestly, including if you aren't sure what the Spirit's work looks like for you.

Paul lists "love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control" (vv. 22, 23). Which one do you most see growing in someone you know, and which would you most like to see more of in yourself?
5.life: Pick one quality from the fruit of the Spirit list that you need most right now. Each morning this week, ask God to grow it in you, and at the end of the week note one moment where you saw even a small sign of it.
5.prayer: Thank God for the freedom Christ has given. Ask the Spirit to help each person in the group use that freedom to serve others in love, and to grow the kind of fruit only he can grow.
5.tip: The list of the flesh in verses 19 to 21 can feel like a checklist for judging others or ourselves. Point out that it includes things like jealousy, rivalries and factions alongside the more obvious items, and keep bringing the group back to verse 22 and to grace: the Spirit grows fruit, we don't manufacture it.

6.open: Think of a time someone helped you carry something heavy, whether a move, a hard season, or a literal load. What made that help feel good?
questions: Paul says if someone is "caught in a trespass," restore him "with a spirit of gentleness" (v. 1). The word for restore was used for setting a broken bone. What would careful, gentle repair look like with a friend who has slipped?
The same verse adds, "But watch yourself, or you also may be tempted" (v. 1). How does remembering our own weak spots change the way we treat someone who has failed?
Paul says, "Carry one another's burdens," and calls this fulfilling "the law of Christ" (v. 2). When has someone carried a burden for you, and what did it mean to you?
Verse 5 says "each one should carry his own load," which sounds different from verse 2. How do you tell the difference between a burden you should share and a load that is yours to carry?
Paul warns that "if anyone thinks he is something when he is nothing, he deceives himself" (v. 3). Where are you most tempted to measure yourself against other people?

Verse 9 says, "Let us not grow weary in well-doing." Where do you feel tired of doing good right now, and what would help you keep going? Feel free to answer honestly if the real answer is that you doubt it is worth it.
Paul says "God is not to be mocked. Whatever a man sows, he will reap in return" (v. 7). What does it look like in daily life to sow "to please the Spirit" instead of the flesh (v. 8)?
Paul says, "may I never boast, except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ" (v. 14). What do people around us boast in, and what would it mean to boast in the cross instead?
6.life: Pick one person who seems to be carrying something heavy, and do one practical thing for them this week, such as a meal, a call, or an hour of your time. Do it quietly, without needing credit.
6.prayer: Thank God for the grace that Paul wishes for his readers in the last verse. Ask for gentleness toward people who stumble, and for the strength not to grow weary in doing good.
6.tip: Verses 2 and 5 can sound like they contradict each other, and verse 7 can be heard as a warning that crushes people who feel they have already failed. Explain that Paul is separating burdens too big to carry alone from personal responsibility, and that he writes verse 7 to people already held by grace, so keep verses 14 to 15 and the closing blessing in view.
